newsitem.title: UK: Most African air safety is appalling, say pilots.
newsitem.headline: Most African air safety is appalling, say pilots.

text.p: Airline safety over most of Africa is appalling and a mid-air collision is just waiting to happen, the world's airline pilots said on Wednesday.

The International Federation of Airline Pilots' Associations (IFALPA) reported a marked increase in near-misses over Africa this year and said pilots rather than air traffic controllers were often responsible for avoiding collisions.

"IFALPA believes that the situation in the African region has become untenable and that a mid air-collision has only been avoided by the most fortuitous circumstances," said the body which groups 100,000 pilots in 90 countries.

"At least 75 percent of the air traffic infrastructure in Africa is unable to provide the services that are required for the safe and expeditious operation of flights through their area of responsibility," it said.
IFALPA declared the entire continent to be critically deficient with the exception of South Africa, Botswana, Namibia, ZImbabwe, Egypt, the Western Saharan region and Morocco.

Many regions did not provide any air traffic control at all to jets en route to other destinations, forcing pilots to broadcast regular updates of where they were to other aircraft in the area to avoid mid-air smashes.

IFALPA said the problems stemmed from a 300 percent increase in traffic between Europe and South Africa over the last two years and urged carriers operating over Africa to fit anti-collision devices to their aircraft.

IFALPA said flights over Africa were "inherently at risk" because of inadequate or non-existent air traffic control systems, poor controller training and the fact that aircraft in the region often lacked crucial safety equipment.
"This situation, coupled with a demand for more traffic in the region, increases the risk on a daily basis of a tragic accident or incident occurring," it said.
"Giving the flying public and pilots the impression they are flying through an area in which their flight is continually regulated and safeguarded could not be farther from the truth."
IFALPA told its members to be extra vigilant until standards were improved and issued a damning list of deficiencies which could be experienced in much of Africa.
Weather information provided by local air traffic control was often inaccurate and there were high concentrations of birds at many airports, it said.

IFALPA warned pilots that their brakes could be rendered useless by the large amounts of rubber left on runways and told them to keep a close eye out for stray people, animals and vehicles while on the ground.
Many runways were covered in debris or breaking up and pilots operating at night should be aware that runway, taxiway and apron lighting was often inadequate, it said.

British pilots on Saturday called for urgent action to stem what they described as an alarming rate of air disasters around the world and said they were particularly worried about air safety in Africa.
